reasoning: Retained all three distinct coverage gaps: conventional referents for figurative object labels, role-versus-example distinctions, and quotations cut off mid-phrase. These edits target separate text regions and do not duplicate the skill's existing broader rules. Each is supported by one of the two source patches.

edits.target: - Treat terse statements, quoted fragments, and incomplete phrases as information-seeking clues when appropriate. Infer the answer slot from the wording, then use the context to identify the entity or value that satisfies the clue.
edits.content: - When a clue uses a quoted or figurative label for an object, resolve its conventional referent instead of guessing a merely plausible object from the setting. Check that the candidate fits the practical details of the described event.

edits.target: - Track the clue's relationships carefully: distinguish a place from its country, a performer from a tribute act, and a quoted hint from its concrete referent. Do not answer with a nearby topic, merely repeat the clue, or respond True/False unless the prompt actually asks for a yes/no judgment.
edits.content: - In wording such as “this [role or category], like [named person],” treat the named person as an example used to identify the requested role or category; answer that role or category, not the example.

edits.target: - When an ellipsis marks omitted words in a title or phrase, use context to recover and return the missing continuation. Prefer a completion that fits the whole fragment over a prominent work or entity that matches only a shorter substring.
edits.content: - When an ellipsis or a quotation cut off mid-phrase marks omitted words, use context to recover and return the missing continuation. If the clue quotes a passage and asks what comes next, complete the quoted wording rather than naming its work or author. Prefer a completion that fits the whole fragment over a prominent work or entity that matches only a shorter substring.
